title: The history of noodles
tagline: From a 4,000-year-old bowl in China to 124 billion instant servings a year: how strands of dough were pulled, pressed, dried, fried and carried around the world.
intro: Nobody invented the noodle once. Cooks in China, India, the Middle East and Italy each found ways to turn dough into strands, and the oldest evidence is still argued over. What changed everything was machinery: the press in Naples, the dryer, and in 1958 a pan of hot oil in a shed in Japan.

eras.name: Dough, long before recipes
eras.summary: A bowl of ancient strands in China, wheat 'soup cakes' in Han poems, pressed rice strings in the Tamil south and boiled dough in Palestine. The evidence is thin and often argued over.

eras.name: Dried strands that travel
eras.summary: Dried pasta appears in Arabic dictionaries and in Sicily's export trade. In India a cookbook describes a press for rice strings, and a Persian cold noodle sweet moves east.

eras.name: Presses, pullers and stalls
eras.summary: Naples puts a press to work and pasta becomes street food. Chinese cooks carry noodles to Calcutta and Tokyo, a Lanzhou cook sells hand-pulled beef noodles, and factories learn to dry pasta in any weather.

eras.name: The instant age
eras.summary: A shed in Ikeda, Japan produces a fried noodle block that cooks in hot water. Within 30 years it is made in Indonesia, India, Nepal and far beyond.

eras.name: Standards, space and scrutiny
eras.summary: Makers form a world association, noodles get an international food standard and a trip to orbit, and a recall in India shows how much depends on lab tests and labels.

events.title: A bowl of 4,000-year-old noodles
events.who: People of the Qijia culture; reported by Lu Houyuan and colleagues
events.text: Archaeologists found long, thin yellow strands inside an upturned bowl buried under about 3 metres of sediment. Lu Houyuan's team reported them in Nature in October 2005 as noodles made from broomcorn and foxtail millet, about 4,000 years old. Other researchers later questioned whether millet could have made them (see 2011).
events.why: It is the oldest claimed physical find of noodles anywhere, and it is still debated.

events.date: c. 1st century CE (as read by K. T. Achaya)
events.title: Rice strings in the Tamil south
events.who: Sangam-era poets, as read by food historian K. T. Achaya
events.text: Idiyappam is rice dough pressed into fine strings and steamed. The food historian K. T. Achaya wrote that idiyappam and appam were known in the Tamil country around the 1st century CE, going by references in Sangam literature. The dating of those poems is itself approximate, so the claim is best treated as his reading.
events.why: It suggests pressed rice noodles in South India may be as old as wheat noodles in Han China.

events.title: A Han dictionary defines 'bing'
events.who: Liu Xi, compiler of the Shiming
events.text: The earliest written record of noodles in China comes from the Eastern Han period (25–220 CE). The dictionary Shiming, from about 200 CE, uses the word bing for foods made of wheat dough. Boiled strips of dough were called tang bing, which means 'soup cake'.
events.why: It is the first time noodles show up in writing, as one member of a big family of dough foods.

events.title: Shu Xi writes an ode to dough
events.text: The scholar Shu Xi wrote a long poem known as the 'Ode to Bing' or 'Rhapsody on Bing'. It lists many kinds of dough food and says which suits each season. Boiled noodles in hot broth are his choice for winter.
events.why: It is one of the earliest detailed descriptions of how noodles were made and eaten.

events.title: Itrium in Palestine, itriyya in Arabic
events.who: Compilers of the Jerusalem Talmud; later the physician Isho bar Ali
events.text: The Jerusalem Talmud mentions itrium, a kind of boiled dough eaten in Palestine between the 3rd and 5th centuries. In the 9th century the physician and dictionary writer Isho bar Ali defined the Arabic word itriyya as string-like shapes of semolina, dried before cooking.
events.why: Bar Ali's definition is among the earliest clear descriptions of dried pasta, the kind that keeps and travels.

events.title: A Kannada cookbook describes the noodle press
events.who: Chavundaraya II, author of the Lokopakara (attributed)
events.text: The Lokopakara, a Kannada text dated to about 1025, describes how to make shavige and the mould used to press it. Shavige, sevai and idiyappam are regional names for strings of rice dough pushed through small holes.
events.why: It is an early written description of extruding: forcing dough through a die to shape it.

events.title: Al-Idrisi sees pasta shipped from Sicily
events.who: Muhammad al-Idrisi, geographer at the court of Roger II
events.text: In his geography of 1154, al-Idrisi wrote that at Trabia, near Palermo, vast quantities of itriyya were made and exported everywhere. This was in Norman Sicily, more than a century before Marco Polo was born.
events.why: It is the first clear record of pasta made in bulk for trade in what is now Italy.

events.title: Faloodeh becomes falooda
events.who: Persian and Mughal court cooks (attributed)
events.text: Faloodeh is a Persian frozen sweet of thin starch noodles in rose-water syrup, linked especially with Shiraz. Popular accounts say it reached India with Persian-speaking courts and became falooda in the Mughal period, with milk and basil seeds added later. The dates are tradition, not firm record.
events.why: It shows noodles are not always savoury, and not always hot.

events.title: Naples puts a press to work
events.who: Neapolitan pasta makers
events.text: In the 1600s, pasta makers in Naples began using a kneading machine and a mechanical press that pushed dough through a die. Pasta got cheaper as meat got scarcer for the poor. Neapolitans, once nicknamed 'leaf eaters', were being called 'macaroni eaters' by the 1700s.
events.why: Machines turned pasta from a treat for the rich into everyday street food.

events.title: A Chinese settler founds Achipur
events.who: Tong Atchew (Yang Dazhao)
events.text: Around 1778, Tong Atchew was granted 650 bighas of land by Governor-General Warren Hastings, at a rent of 45 rupees a year, to set up a sugar mill south of Calcutta. He died in 1783 and the settlement broke up, but his workers and later arrivals moved into the city. The place is still called Achipur.
events.why: Calcutta's Chinese community grew from here, and with it the hakka noodles and 'Indian Chinese' food eaten across India today.

events.title: Family pasta firms and a dryer that beats the weather
events.who: Giulia Buitoni; Pietro Barilla; Filippo De Cecco
events.where: Sansepolcro, Parma and Fara San Martino
events.text: Giulia Buitoni opened a pasta shop in Sansepolcro in 1827. Pietro Barilla opened a bread and pasta shop in Parma in 1877. De Cecco, founded in 1886 at Fara San Martino, says Filippo De Cecco built a low-temperature hot-air dryer, so pasta no longer depended on sun and wind.
events.why: Controlled drying let pasta be made anywhere, in any season, and shipped far.

events.title: Rairaiken serves Chinese noodles in Tokyo
events.who: Kan'ichi Ozaki and twelve Cantonese cooks
events.text: Chinese noodle soups had reached Japan through Yokohama's Chinatown in the late 1800s. In 1910 Kan'ichi Ozaki opened Rairaiken in Asakusa with twelve Cantonese cooks and sold the dish as 'shina soba'. It is often called Japan's first ramen shop.
events.why: It marks the start of ramen as a Japanese dish and not only a Chinese import.

events.title: Ma Baozi sells hand-pulled beef noodles
events.who: Ma Baozi (attributed)
events.text: Historians often credit Ma Baozi, a Hui Muslim cook, with selling Lanzhou beef noodle soup in its modern form from about 1915. The noodles are lamian: dough stretched and folded by hand into finer and finer strands. An alkaline ingredient makes the dough stretchy. In ramen the same job is done by kansui, a mix of sodium and potassium carbonates.
events.why: Hand-pulling shows what gluten can do, and alkaline water is why ramen is yellow and springy.

events.title: Eau Chew and the Chinese kitchens of Calcutta
events.who: Achumpa Huang and family; later Nelson Wang in Bombay
events.text: Eau Chew, opened in the 1920s as an eating house for Chinese migrants, is described as India's oldest family-run Chinese restaurant. Tangra grew into a second Chinatown in the same years. Cooks adjusted Cantonese and Hakka dishes to local tastes. In Bombay, Nelson Wang says he invented chicken Manchurian at the Cricket Club of India in 1975.
events.why: This is the root of hakka noodles and chow mein as Indian street food.

events.title: The Marco Polo myth is printed
events.who: The Macaroni Journal, a US pasta trade magazine
events.text: A story in the Macaroni Journal told how a sailor with Marco Polo found noodles in China and brought them home. It was a piece of trade publicity, but the tale stuck. Pasta was in Italy long before Polo returned in 1295: al-Idrisi described Sicily's trade in 1154, and a document from Genoa in the 1270s lists a basket of macaroni.
events.why: The best-known 'fact' about noodles is a 20th-century invention.

events.title: Cheap wheat and ramen stalls
events.who: Street vendors in occupied Japan
events.text: After the war Japan had its worst rice harvest in decades. The United States supplied cheap wheat flour, and ramen stalls spread through the cities.
events.why: Wheat noodles became everyday food in Japan, setting the scene for the instant kind.

events.title: Chicken Ramen: the first instant noodle
events.who: Momofuku Ando, with his wife Masako Ando
events.text: Ando worked for about a year in a small shed behind his house in Ikeda. He is said to have got the key idea from watching his wife Masako fry tempura: hot oil drives the water out of the noodles and leaves tiny holes that let hot water back in. Nissin launched Chicken Ramen on 25 August 1958. At 35 yen it cost about six times as much as fresh noodles.
events.why: Flash-frying made a cooked noodle that keeps for months and is ready in minutes.

events.title: Cup Noodles: the pack is the bowl
events.who: Momofuku Ando and Nissin
events.text: On a sales trip to the United States in 1966, Ando saw buyers break his noodles into a paper cup and eat them with a fork. Cup Noodles went on sale in September 1971. Sales were slow until February 1972, when live television of the Asama-Sanso hostage siege showed riot police eating them in the freezing cold.
events.why: The cup removed the last need: a pot and a bowl.

events.title: Indomie, and later Mi Goreng
events.who: PT Sanmaru Food Manufacturing; later Indofood
events.text: Indomie was first made in June 1972, with a chicken broth flavour. In 1982 the brand launched Mi Goreng, a dry version based on Indonesian fried noodles (some accounts say 1983). Exports reached Nigeria in 1988, and a factory opened there in 1995.
events.why: It showed that instant noodles could take on a local dish and then travel the world with it.

events.title: Maggi 2-Minute Noodles reach India
events.who: Nestlé India; marketing team including Sangeeta Talwar
events.text: Nestlé India launched Maggi noodles in 1983 (a few business case studies say 1982). It was sold on a simple promise, '2-minute noodles', with the flavour in a separate tastemaker sachet. Instant noodles were almost unknown in India then. For years afterwards Maggi held most of the market.
events.why: It turned a foreign product into an Indian habit, and 'Maggi' into a common word for instant noodles.

events.title: Wai Wai comes to Nepal
events.who: Binod Chaudhary and the Chaudhary Group
events.text: Wai Wai began in Thailand in 1972. Binod Chaudhary noticed travellers bringing packets home from Bangkok and struck a deal with the Thai maker for technical help. The Chaudhary Group began making Wai Wai in Nepal in 1984 or 1985: sources give both years. The noodle is already seasoned and fried, so many people eat it dry as a snack.
events.why: Nepal became one of the keenest instant noodle countries, and Wai Wai is now made in India too.

events.title: Top Ramen arrives, and the Indian shelf fills up
events.who: Indo Nissin Foods; later ITC
events.text: Nissin, the company that invented instant noodles, entered India in 1991 with Top Ramen. ITC launched Sunfeast Yippee! in September 2010. Maggi stayed in front, but it now had rivals.
events.why: Competition brought new shapes, flavours and prices to Indian instant noodles.

events.title: The makers form a world association
events.who: Momofuku Ando and noodle makers from several countries
events.text: At the first World Ramen Summit in Tokyo, makers set up the International Ramen Manufacturers Association, with Ando as its first chairman. It was later renamed the World Instant Noodles Association (WINA). It publishes the yearly count of servings eaten in each country.
events.why: The industry gained a shared voice on quality and safety, and a shared set of numbers.

events.title: Instant noodles go to space
events.who: Soichi Noguchi, Nissin and JAXA
events.text: Nissin and Japan's space agency JAXA developed Space Ram: ball-shaped noodles in a thick soup that will not float away, made to soften in water at about 70°C. Astronaut Soichi Noguchi took it on Discovery's STS-114 flight, launched on 26 July 2005. Nissin says he was the first person to eat instant noodles in space.
events.why: It was Ando's last big project. He died on 5 January 2007, aged 96.

events.title: A world standard for instant noodles
events.who: Codex Alimentarius Commission (FAO and WHO)
events.text: The Codex Alimentarius Commission adopted the Standard for Instant Noodles, CXS 249-2006. It covers fried and non-fried instant noodles, with or without seasoning sachets, and it does not apply to pasta. It has been amended several times since.
events.why: Countries now had a common reference for what an instant noodle is and how it should be tested.

events.title: The Lajia noodles are questioned
events.who: Wei Ge, Li Liu, Xingcan Chen and Zhengyao Jin
events.text: Four researchers tried to make noodles from millet and published the results in the journal Archaeometry. They reported that pure millet dough cannot be stretched into noodles, because millet has no gluten. They also argued that the millet husks and starch grains found at Lajia may not have been part of the strands at all.
events.why: It keeps the oldest noodle claim open: something was in the bowl, but what it was made of is unsettled.

events.title: Maggi is withdrawn across India
events.who: Uttar Pradesh food safety officers; FSSAI; Nestlé India
events.text: A food inspector in Barabanki, Uttar Pradesh, sent a packet labelled 'No added MSG' for testing; press reports date the sample to March 2014. A state lab reported MSG. A referral lab in Kolkata then reported lead of about 17 parts per million, against a limit of 2.5. In early June 2015 several states banned the noodles. Nestlé India announced a withdrawal overnight on 4–5 June, saying the product was safe, and on 5 June the food regulator FSSAI ordered all nine variants recalled.
events.why: It became one of the largest food recalls in India: about 38,000 tonnes were destroyed, much of it burned as fuel in cement kilns.

events.title: The court sets the ban aside, and Maggi returns
events.who: Bombay High Court (Justices V. M. Kanade and B. P. Colabawalla)
events.text: On 13 August 2015 the Bombay High Court quashed the orders of 5 and 6 June. It held that Nestlé had not been given a fair hearing and that the labs relied on were not properly accredited. It ordered fresh tests at three accredited labs, in Mohali, Hyderabad and Jaipur, within six weeks. On 16 October Nestlé India said all 90 samples had come back with lead well within the limit. Maggi went back on sale on 9 November 2015.
events.why: The case turned on procedure and lab accreditation, and it led to closer attention to how food is sampled and tested.

events.title: A label rule and a revived claim
events.who: FSSAI; Supreme Court of India; consumer affairs ministry
events.text: In an order dated 31 March 2016, FSSAI said no lab test can tell added MSG from the glutamate that occurs naturally in foods, and that action would follow only where a pack claims 'No MSG' and MSG is found. Separately, the government had filed a class action in 2015 at the national consumer commission (NCDRC), seeking about Rs 640 crore from Nestlé India. The Supreme Court had stayed it. On 3 January 2019 the court let it go ahead, on the basis of test reports from the CFTRI lab in Mysuru.
events.why: The episode changed what Indian noodle packs say about MSG, and its legal tail ran for years.

events.title: 124 billion servings in a year
events.who: World Instant Noodles Association
events.text: WINA estimates that the world ate about 124.2 billion servings of instant noodles in 2025. China with Hong Kong came first at 43.3 billion, then Indonesia at 14.5 billion. India ate about 9.6 billion, up from 7.6 billion in 2021, and Nepal about 1.6 billion.
events.why: A food invented in a garden shed in 1958 is now eaten more than 300 million times a day.

people.name: Muhammad al-Idrisi

people.name: Giulia Buitoni
people.note: Opened a pasta shop in 1827 to support her family; it grew into the Buitoni company.

people.name: Tong Atchew (Yang Dazhao)
people.note: Remembered as the first Chinese settler near Calcutta; Achipur is named after him.

people.name: Ma Baozi
people.note: Credited by many historians with the modern form of Lanzhou hand-pulled beef noodles.

people.name: Momofuku Ando
people.note: Invented instant noodles at 48 and Cup Noodles at 61, and led the makers' world association.

people.name: Masako Ando
people.note: Her tempura frying is credited, in the usual telling, with giving Ando the idea of flash-frying noodles.

facts: In a survey by the Fuji Research Institute in 2000, adults in Japan named instant noodles the best Japanese invention of the 20th century. Karaoke came second.
Chinese texts once used a single word, bing, for noodles, dumplings, buns and flatbreads alike. What mattered was that they were made of wheat dough.
The last day of the Asama-Sanso siege in 1972 was shown live on Japanese television for 10 hours and 40 minutes. Viewers saw riot police eating Cup Noodles in the snow.
In 2022 UNESCO added the Pyongyang raengmyon custom, cold buckwheat noodles served in a brass bowl, to its list of intangible cultural heritage.
One common story says rice noodles began when northern Chinese wheat-eaters moved south in the Qin dynasty and made noodles from the local grain instead. It is a tradition, not a dated record.
The word noodle in this history covers three different tricks: wheat held together by gluten, rice or bean starch set by heat, and dough fried so that water can rush back in.
